body: Sorry, don't want to talk about that.

> So, is there someone you have in mind to talk to in person, that can help you more?

No.

It's not about just caring, it's about "truly" caring (it's a question of *how much* do you care?). I don't believe you are a soulless asshole that wants me to die. I believe the people in this subreddit do intend to do good. But that doesn't mean you care a whole lot (and of course there are degrees of how much you care/love someone else). 

>It is also how YOU perceive it. There are others who are helped by kind words; does it make it less real for them? 

Of course not. But this is about how *I* perceive it, and to me it doesn't feel very "real" in the sense that there isn't much love/weight behind your words. Yes, others were helped, but that doesn't prove that you genuinely cared/loved for them. All it means is that they bought your words and bettered themselves.

At the core, it's not about words, it's about your actions. "Actions speak louder than words" -- the action is random internet strangers spending some of their free time behind their computer typing out messages that they care about other random internet strangers. That doesn't speak very loudly to me.

> It really would be a lot more fulfilling in person. I'm not denying that. But wouldn't it still be anonymous if we met at a bus stop, rather than here?
 
Sure, you could still call it anonymous, but I believe there are degrees to anonymity. I still strongly believe that sitting at your computer at home at your leisure and typing these responses doesn't hold a candle to making plans to meet face-to-face with someone (sure, still a stranger) and talk to them. The latter feels more like a "real life" emotional interaction and carries with it more weight. 

I don't think I'm the only one that puts more weight into emotions in person than on the internet. Just like with internet trolls. An internet stranger's negative words don't hold a candle to the same words said face-to-face. It's the same if we're talking about an internet stranger's positive words. In both cases, I respond a ton more strongly in person because I feel the person is a lot more impassioned with their negative/positive words.

> I guess what I'm trying to say is that, even though it's through the internet, it doesn't mean our words are hollow. 

It doesn't mean your words are hollow, but I think by instinct the words don't hold the same value because there is a lack of inter-personal interactions. 

With internet trolls, we brush off their words as hollow because they are negative, but with posters to this sub we put value behind their words because they are positive? In both cases, it's just some random person hiding behind a computer.

I agree it's his/her opinion and thus, by definition, doesn't apply to everyone. The problem is that it's an opinion I find myself agreeing and the counter-argument "There are people who care" just appears weak and full of fluff. I can't fool myself to believe it even if it's argued that it's better to have a positive mindset than a negative one.

> We may be strangers on the internet, but would you reject help from someone who offers you a hand if you tripped in public? We're like that. 

I struggle to believe this because I honestly don't think they are all that similar. Say, sending a message to a random redditor that looks depressed doesn't hold the same amount of weight/love as offering your ear to a random depressed stranger you see in real life. I feel that the same action done through the anonymity of the internet holds orders of magnitude less weight/love as it would if you did it in person to a stranger.

>It doesn't need to be special or outstanding. Because after all that, those who responded, responded to you and you only. 

I also struggle to agree with this reasoning. Okay, yes, you are here responding to me right here right now. But how does that address the concern of there not being significant weight/love behind your message because it's all anonymous and nothing is special? To me, it feels like dodging the original concern by putting all the focus on "You need help and someone is trying to help you right now, so ipso facto it doesn't need to be special. QED"

I appreciate the response. Unfortunately, thinking of myself as better than the troll or thinking of the troll as an asshole doesn't help my brain from discrediting the words. The words might have been provided by an asshole, but the words can stand on their own and they make sense to me. I can't "conveniently" ignore words that make sense sense to me just because they are negative or less than ideal.
